solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: A second Lincoln’s toppled and I’m in a cell for life

definitions.text: I’m in a cell for life

indicators.note: in a down entry a toppled statue ends upside down, so the name is read bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
a mo is a moment, a second
Abe is Abraham Lincoln's familiar name; the 's means 'is'

explanation.surface: A prisoner reflects that, after a president's fall, they are locked up for good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a cell for life' suggests a life sentence, but the speaker is a single-celled creature living its whole life in one cell.
explanation.definitionFit: An amoeba is a single-celled organism, so its whole existence is spent within one microscopic unit.

clue.text: Rest in diving area when energy’s spent

indicators.note: energy that is spent has been used up and is gone, so its letter leaves

blocks.note: the deep end of a pool is where people dive
E is the symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A tired swimmer takes a breather in the deep end once their energy runs out.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the two Es in DEEP END is lost, leaving DEPEND.
explanation.definitionFit: To depend on something is to rest on it, relying on it for support, as an argument rests on evidence.

clue.text: PVC component your old boy put in within limits of estimate

indicators.note: something put in within a pair of letters sits between them
the limits of a word are its two ends, so only the outside letters count

blocks.note: first part of the outer pair of this word
thy is the old form of your
Len, short for Leonard, is a boy's name
last part of the outer pair of this word

explanation.surface: A chemistry recipe for plastic, with a family member's name slipped in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Your old boy' reads as a son or old schoolboy, but it splits into an archaic pronoun and a short boy's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethylene is the hydrocarbon from which vinyl chloride, and so polyvinyl chloride plastic, is manufactured.

clue.text: Somewhat malevolent creature

indicators.note: somewhat means only a part of the following word, so a stretch of its letters is used

blocks.note: the letters sit inside this word, after MALE

explanation.surface: A description of a rather nasty animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A vole is a small rodent, a field creature something like a mouse with a blunter snout.

clue.text: When at sea I travel North-East and run off the point

indicators.note: to be at sea is to be confused and lost, so these letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written
compass abbreviation
compass abbreviation
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for a run

explanation.surface: A sailor describes heading north-east and running off a headland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Point' looks like a headland on the voyage; here it is the point of an argument.
explanation.definitionFit: Something irrelevant is beside the matter under discussion, having no bearing on the central issue.

clue.text: Racket’s not caught the second one

indicators.note: the noise is said to be without, not having, the letter that follows

blocks.note: a clatter is a racket, a loud noise; the 's means 'is'
c is the cricket scoring abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A tennis player's racket fails to catch the second ball.
explanation.walkthrough: CLATTER loses its C. Racket is the noise, not a tennis racket.
explanation.definitionFit: Of two things mentioned, the latter is the one named second, as opposed to the former.

clue.text: In Woodstock we are this – beginning to catch Diamonds and Rust essentially

indicators.note: the first word is to catch the following letters, holding them inside itself
the essence of a word is taken as its core, its middle letters

blocks.note: a start is a beginning
D is the card abbreviation for diamonds
the middle letters of this word

explanation.surface: Music trivia linking Joni Mitchell's Woodstock and Joan Baez's Diamonds and Rust.
explanation.walkthrough: Joni Mitchell's song Woodstock runs 'We are stardust, we are golden'; 24 down shares this definition. Diamonds and Rust is a Joan Baez song, used here only for its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The lyric of the Woodstock song declares that we are stardust, so this word completes the quoted line.

clue.text: Some resistance met finally with a bad conductor

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word before it
bad letters are faulty and need putting right, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the symbol for electrical resistance
the last letter of this word
taken as written

explanation.surface: An electrical scene: resistance meets a poor conductor of current.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resistance' and 'conductor' look like physics; the conductor is a musician leading an orchestra.
explanation.definitionFit: Maestro is the honorific used for an eminent orchestra leader, so it stands for someone who directs musicians.

clue.text: Hurt perhaps following faithful instruction in nuclear facility

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the performer is placed behind the schooling

blocks.note: RE is religious education, a school subject
William or John Hurt, both actors

explanation.surface: Someone injured after following religious teaching at a nuclear plant.
explanation.walkthrough: Hurt is the surname of the actors John and William Hurt, not an injury; RE is school religious education.
explanation.definitionFit: A reactor is the installation where a controlled nuclear chain reaction is run, typically to generate power.

clue.text: Stay inside always retiring in comfort

indicators.note: inside places the first word within the second
retiring means going back, so in this down entry the word reads upward

blocks.note: ever means always
to lie is to stay, remain at rest

explanation.surface: Advice to stay in and always go to bed in comfort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stay inside' reads as staying indoors, but stay is the word placed inside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: To relieve someone is to ease their distress or pain, which is what comforting them does.

clue.text: Famous one for example set in rural church domain

indicators.note: something set in a place is lodged inside it

blocks.note: eg is the abbreviation for for example
Ely is a cathedral city and diocese in the Cambridgeshire fens

explanation.surface: A famous example of something set in a country churchyard.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue nods to Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard, the most famous poem of its kind, whose setting the surface describes.
explanation.definitionFit: Gray's Elegy is perhaps the best-known English poem, so a famous one names this mournful poetic form.

clue.text: Before joining left, tragic daughter has nothing to do with voting

indicators.note: the daughter has, or holds, the next item within her
she comes before, and is then joined by, the following letter

blocks.note: Electra, daughter of Agamemnon, is a heroine of Greek tragedy
O looks like zero
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A tragic daughter refuses to vote before joining the Left.
explanation.walkthrough: O goes inside ELECTRA, then L follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Electoral describes anything relating to elections, the process by which citizens cast ballots.

clue.text: He’s written to Doctor S in a letter

indicators.note: in places the first pair of items inside the second pair

blocks.note: taken as written
the name of the letter D
Dr is the abbreviation for doctor
the spelt-out name of the letter S

explanation.surface: A man who receives a letter from someone called Doctor S.
explanation.walkthrough: Both letters are spelt out as their names, a common crossword trick; 'Doctor S' looks like a person but is two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The addressee is the person to whom a letter or parcel is directed, its intended recipient.

clue.text: Help for climber very inclined to lose heart, left hanging over the summer

indicators.note: losing heart means the middle letter drops out
in a down entry what hangs over something sits above it

blocks.note: steep means sharply sloping
L is the abbreviation for left
someone who sums, or adds up, is an adder

explanation.surface: A mountaineer on a steep slope loses heart, left dangling all summer.
explanation.walkthrough: STEEP loses its middle E. 'Summer' is not the season but one who sums: an adder.
explanation.definitionFit: A stepladder is a folding set of steps that lets someone reach higher shelves or ceilings, aiding anyone who climbs.

clue.text: We hear what US cheerleaders do – “Way to go!”

indicators.note: we hear means the word is identified by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: Americans root for a team when they cheer it on

explanation.surface: Cheerleaders shouting encouragement: 'Way to go!'
explanation.walkthrough: The homophone works in American speech, where the two words are said alike; to root for a team is to cheer it.
explanation.definitionFit: A route is the path or road one takes to reach a destination, hence a way to go.

clue.text: This company greet perhaps when distraught

definitions.text: This company greet perhaps when distraught

indicators.note: distraught means torn apart with grief, so these letters are disordered

blocks.note: Co is the abbreviation for company
taken as written

explanation.surface: A group of mourners who weep in their distress.
explanation.walkthrough: Greet is Scots for weep, so the whole clue describes mourners weeping, while CO plus a shuffle of GREET builds the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A cortege is a funeral procession, a body of mourners who might well weep in their grief.

clue.text: Newspaper articles for such as the Standard?

blocks.note: first meaning: regular pieces by a newspaper writer
second meaning: upright supports, of which a standard is one

explanation.walkthrough: The Standard looks like London's Evening Standard newspaper; here a standard is an upright pole or post.
explanation.definitionFit: Columns are both regular newspaper features by one writer and vertical pillars, like a standard upright.

clue.text: Drunk a beer after taking ecstasy, requiring service to imbibe again

indicators.note: after something is taken away it is no longer there, so its letter goes
drunk letters stagger out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
E is slang for the drug ecstasy
the service tree is also called the sorb

explanation.surface: A drinker who took ecstasy now needs a service to sober up.
explanation.walkthrough: One E goes from A BEER, the rest is shuffled, and SORB follows. The service tree, a relative of the rowan, is also called the sorb.
explanation.definitionFit: To reabsorb is to take something in once more, just as imbibing means soaking up or drinking.

clue.text: Eg St Paul‘s epistle with a couple of misprints?

indicators.note: two misprints means two letters of the word are swapped for different ones

blocks.note: a letter, as in the epistles of the New Testament

explanation.surface: A scholar notes typos in one of St Paul's letters.
explanation.walkthrough: Change the first E to A and the I to O in EPISTLE. St Paul wrote many epistles, which fits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul is counted among the apostles, the first missionaries who spread Christian teaching.

clue.text: Make light work – to repeat, it’s broken

definitions.note: read as a noun phrase: a make, or kind, of light work

indicators.note: something broken is in pieces, ready to be put back together in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone told to do a task easily keeps having to repeat it because it broke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make light work' reads as the idiom for doing a job easily; here it is a light musical work.
explanation.definitionFit: An operetta is a short, light-hearted opera with spoken dialogue, a lighter piece of musical theatre.

clue.text: Animal left over after new one’s taken as beast of burden

indicators.note: turned over means the remaining letters read backwards
the letters are read after something has been taken from them
taken away means those letters are removed

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for left
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new
I is the Roman numeral one; the 's means 'is'

explanation.surface: A leftover animal is put to work carrying loads after a new one arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: ANIMAL loses N and I, leaving AMAL, which is reversed and put after L. 'Animal' looks like the definition; it is the raw word to be worked.
explanation.definitionFit: Llamas are South American camelids kept to carry packs over mountain terrain, so they are pack animals.

clue.text: She studied a compound with sodium

blocks.note: alum is a chemical compound, a double sulphate
Na is the chemical symbol for sodium

explanation.surface: A woman who did chemistry, working on a sodium compound.
explanation.definitionFit: An alumna is a female former student of a school or university, so she studied there.

clue.text: He’s wrong to drop US dance craze – Jack’s gone for Latin

indicators.note: one letter has gone and another is in its place, swapped for it

blocks.note: the jitterbug was a lively American swing dance of the 1930s and 40s
J is the card abbreviation for jack
L is the abbreviation for Latin

explanation.surface: Someone is wrong to abandon an American dance craze in favour of Latin dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: In JITTERBUG the J is replaced by L. 'Drop' looks like giving up the dance; it means dropping rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: A litterbug carelessly throws rubbish on the ground, doing wrong by leaving waste lying about.

clue.text: Dog held up fleece, one ounce over

indicators.note: held up in a down entry means lifted, so the word reads from the bottom
turned over means these letters read the other way

blocks.note: to fleece someone is to rob them
Roman numeral one
oz is the abbreviation for ounce

explanation.surface: A dog is stopped and its coat weighed: an ounce over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Held up' sounds like a hold-up robbery; it reverses ROB. 'Fleece' suggests a woolly coat; it means rob.
explanation.definitionFit: The borzoi is a tall Russian hunting hound bred to course wolves, a breed of sighthound.

clue.text: In Woodstock we are this – spin record for East of Eden

indicators.note: to spin something is to turn it round, so the word reads backwards
for means in place of, so one piece replaces another

blocks.note: a log is a written record
compass abbreviation
taken as written

explanation.surface: A DJ spins a record in place of East of Eden, after quoting the Woodstock song.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversed LOG replaces the first E of EDEN. Joni Mitchell's Woodstock runs 'We are stardust, we are golden'; compare 7 down.
explanation.definitionFit: The Woodstock lyric declares that we are golden, so this word completes the second quoted phrase.

clue.text: Leads up the garden path? I’d guess I’m wrong

indicators.note: letters that are wrong are out of place and need rearranging

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone admits they've been led astray and suspects they're wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: To lead someone up the garden path is the idiom for deceiving them, which is to mislead or misdirect them.

clue.text: Second drink and a kiss and a cuddle

blocks.note: s is the abbreviation for second
nog is a strong ale, or eggnog

explanation.surface: A second drink leads to romance.
explanation.walkthrough: Snog is British slang for a long kiss.
explanation.definitionFit: Snogging is British slang for kissing and cuddling amorously, so the phrase describes it.

clue.text: Learning about new intake and register for classes

indicators.note: an intake is something taken inside, so the letter goes within the word
about as in turned about, so the result reads backwards

blocks.note: lore is learning, accumulated knowledge
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A college's new intake of students learns and signs up for courses.
explanation.walkthrough: N goes inside LORE to make LORNE, which reads backwards. 'Intake' looks like new students; it marks the insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: To enrol is to sign up formally as a member or student, entering one's name for a course.

clue.text: Weird way to travel far and wide

blocks.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way
to range is to roam widely

explanation.surface: A curious method of getting about all over the place.
explanation.definitionFit: Strange and weird both describe something odd, unusual or hard to explain, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Not initially taken by Gay Rabbit? Gone one better

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of the word before it
taken by means held within the following word

blocks.note: openly gay people are out
a doe is a female rabbit
the first letter of this word

explanation.surface: A question about whether the first move was taken by Gay Rabbit, a racehorse or rival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gay Rabbit' reads as a name, but each word gives its own piece; out means openly gay.
explanation.definitionFit: To be outdone is to be surpassed or beaten by someone who has gone further than you.
